headline: 6 Claude Code Skills you should actually install (2026 Edition)
summary: Installing too many Claude Code skills causes unpredictable behavior. This guide identifies 6 essential skills for daily dev work, each mapping to a phase of the development cycle.
details: Claude Code now offers many skills and plugins, but installing them indiscriminately can lead to unpredictable behavior. This guide, based on July 2026 availability, identifies 6 essential skills that significantly improve daily development work.

These 6 skills map to key phases of a typical development cycle: design, implementation, review, security, and testing. It's crucial to install only one skill per phase to prevent Claude from hesitating and causing inconsistent results.

Prioritize official or widely-used plugins for better maintenance and reliability. Only introduce additional skills beyond this core set when you encounter a repetitive task that specifically requires a custom solution.

The 'Superpowers' skill prevents Claude Code from jumping straight to implementation. It forces requirement clarification and root-cause analysis, guiding Claude through a structured process from design to testing. This official plugin was added in January 2026.

The 'Skill-Creator' is an official, widely-used Anthropic plugin that helps you build custom SKILL.md files. It uses an interactive Q&A to generate skill templates tailored to your team's specific workflows.

The 'Frontend-Design' skill, another official Anthropic plugin, generates UI with deliberate aesthetics like brutalism or glassmorphism. Users can specify both the skill and desired style, then refine results with follow-up nudges.

The 'Security-Review' is a free, official Anthropic plugin that scans for 25 vulnerability patterns in real-time during code edits. It also performs LLM-based diff reviews and cross-file checks at commit time, proposing fixes on the spot.

The 'Playwright' skill drives a browser for tasks such as navigation, form input, screenshots, and console log inspection. It can be installed via Microsoft's official Playwright MCP or a token-efficient CLI+Skill setup.

headline_marked: [[Visual QA agents catch UI regressions]] before AI-written code ships, preventing broken interfaces
headline: Visual QA agents catch UI regressions before AI-written code ships, preventing broken interfaces
summary: AI coding agents can ship features with broken UIs despite passing unit tests. Visual QA agents drive apps like users, comparing screenshots and checking flows to prevent regressions.
details: AI coding agents speed up development but can introduce UI regressions, where code compiles and tests pass but the interface is broken. This new failure mode means buttons move, cards overflow, or loading states cover actions.

Visual QA agents address this by performing scoped test missions. They open the app, execute real user journeys, capture evidence, compare against baselines, and report changes. This shifts QA from a manual end-stage pass to an integrated process.

These agents combine browser automation, evidence storage, a "judge" for comparison, and an agent layer for mission generation and failure inspection. The goal is not to replace human judgment but to stop obvious, expensive UI mistakes early.

A practical workflow involves a clear "job contract" for the agent, preventing it from wandering and providing a concrete pass/fail shape for CI systems. The architecture typically includes a browser runner, an evidence store, a comparison judge, and an agent layer.

The browser runner uses tools like Playwright or Cypress to open the app, log in, visit routes, perform actions, and capture screenshots. Evidence should be stored as files and metadata, not just a paragraph, so reviewers have proof with links to screenshots and routes.

The "judge" compares the current run against a baseline using pixel diffing, layout rules, OCR, DOM assertions, or LLM vision checks. Using multiple signals is crucial, as pixel diffs alone can be misleading (e.g., a small copy update causing a big diff).

The AI judge should produce evidence and a risk score, not make final business decisions alone. CI can enforce rules for clearly unsafe states. The agent layer then generates or selects missions, inspects failures, summarizes evidence, and suggests likely causes.
